Use the Evaluations framework to systematically evaluate your app’s intelligence-powered features.
The harder work comes next: making sure your feature handles the full range of inputs it meets in production, and that fixes for one problem don’t silently break cases that already work.
Thinking of your evaluation as your specification forces you to define, from the beginning, exactly what your feature must do, what it must not do, and how you measure the difference.
Different metric types call for different summary statistics: use the mean of pass or fail metrics to get a pass rate directly, and the median of scored metrics to resist outlier skew.

A feature might check format compliance (rule-based), compare answers against known-correct values for a core set (explicit ground truth), and use a model as judge for subjective quality on everything else (no ground truth).
Use a model that is more capable than the model being evaluated as the judge.
Each profile needs at least one sample in your dataset.
The categories below cover the range from cases your feature must always handle to inputs you expect it to refuse.
For each dimension of variation in your feature, include at least one seed that represents each end of the spectrum.

For example, a task-extraction feature might need seeds that cover: Simple and complex inputs Every output category Inputs with and without temporal information Urgent and non-urgent scenarios Ambiguous requests where the correct interpretation requires judgment
A useful guideline is to make at least 20-30 percent of your seeds genuinely difficult cases.
Without them, you get a dataset full of straightforward examples that don’t test your feature’s limits.
Without these, synthetic datasets develop a bias toward always producing a complete, confident answer.
Avoid a single prompt like “generate diverse test cases covering all categories.” That approach produces three problems: Frequency bias.
Use a layered approach: Programmatic validation.
Maintain at least 20-30 percent human-written samples alongside synthetic ones as a calibration anchor.

For multi-step workflows, you can combine expectations: Some tasks require tools to be called in a specific sequence.
Use with an array of entries to enforce ordering: The evaluator scans the transcript sequentially, matching each ordered expectation after the previous one.
Not all workflows require a specific sequence.

Use when only the occurrence of events matters, not the order in which they happen: The evaluator matches each unordered expectation against the entire transcript; position doesn’t matter, only that they happen.

A bedtime routine requires locking the door then dimming the lights (in that order), while closing blinds and adjusting the thermostat can happen at any point: The evaluator checks ordered expectations sequentially, then verifies that every unordered expectation appears somewhere in the transcript.
The model must fully satisfy both sets for the strict metric to pass.
A query that only reads the thermostat must never change settings, even if the model has access to those tools.

specifies expected tool-calling behavior across three axes: Ordered : Tool calls that must occur in a specific sequence.
Use for single sequential steps, or when multiple tools must all be called at a given position but their relative order doesn’t matter.
Unordered : Tool calls that must occur at some point, regardless of when.
Disallowed : Tool calls that must NOT occur.
